generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, the first stage of writing is reading the task closely. A task such as 'Evaluate the main approaches to a problem' carries a steer, the word that tells you how to answer, and keywords that fix what to answer. Here the steer is 'evaluate', which asks you to weigh rather than simply describe. A rough plan then bridges your reading and the writing itself, and a first draft turns that plan into sentences you can improve. Missing the steer is one of the most common and costly mistakes in any subject.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students are set the same task: 'Evaluate the main approaches to a problem in their field.'

Student A reads the task once, spots the topic, and starts writing everything they know about it. They make no plan and pay no attention to the word 'evaluate', so the writing becomes a long description that never weighs the approaches against each other. The steer was missed, and a lot of effort answers a question that was not asked.

Student B reads the task closely, underlines 'evaluate' and the key terms, and notes that the writing must weigh the approaches rather than just list them. A quick plan sets out two approaches, their evidence, and an order. Then Student B writes a rough draft straight from the plan, not worrying yet about style, ready to improve it next.

Both students knew the material. Only Student B read the task, planned, and turned that plan into a draft, the moves that make writing answer the question.
generatedProse.summary: Writing starts with understanding the task: its steer, which tells you how to answer, and its keywords, which fix what to answer. A rough plan then bridges your reading and your writing, and a first draft turns that plan into sentences you can improve. You can now read a task for its steer and keywords, turn a plan into a draft, and make a sensible first move at the blank page. The next lesson is about improving that draft.

check.body: You have read your task and understood what it is asking. What is the most effective next move towards a draft?

items.text: Sketch a rough plan from the task, then write a first draft straight from that plan.
Write down everything you know about the topic without a plan.
Polish your opening paragraph until it is perfect before writing any more.
Wait until you understand the topic completely before writing anything.

feedback.correct: That's right. A rough plan from the task, then a draft straight from the plan, is what turns understanding into writing.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan-then-draft move, rather than a plan-free dump or endless polishing.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The effective move is to plan from the task and draft from the plan. Writing without a plan, perfecting one paragraph, or waiting indefinitely are not it.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
